title: 18F‐FDG PET/CT in early phase of sporadic Creutzfeldt‐Jacob disease: A case report
case_prompt: A 59-year-old previously healthy man was referred for evaluation of a one-month history of rapidly progressive cognitive and motor symptoms. He initially developed akinetic mutism, constructional apraxia, and spatial disorientation, which progressed over weeks to delirium with hallucinations, severe cerebellar ataxia rendering him unable to walk, erratic myoclonus, and rigidity. There was no family history of neurological disease, no substance use, and no recent travel or infections. Neurologic examination on admission showed mild gait ataxia with multidirectional oscillations and cognitive deficits. Routine laboratory studies—including complete blood count, metabolic panel, liver function tests, inflammatory markers, autoimmune antibody panels, viral and bacterial serologies, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis—were all within normal limits. Repetitive electroencephalograms showed no specific abnormalities. Brain MRI with T1, T2, and diffusion-weighted sequences was unremarkable. To further evaluate his condition, a brain 18F-FDG PET/CT scan was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Autoimmune encephalitis, paraneoplastic, and toxic-metabolic encephalopathies were excluded — “All the exams' results were normal, allowing us to exclude autoimmune encephalitis, paraneoplastic and toxic‐metabolic encephalopathies.”  
2. Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body degeneration were considered but ruled out by primary cortical involvement atypical for those conditions — “A primary cortices involvement is also described in CJS and rules out the diagnosis of neurodegenerative syndromes such as Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body degeneration, conditions in which such areas are usually spared.”  
3. Corticobasal degeneration was excluded because, despite the asymmetrical cortical distribution, there was no basal ganglia involvement — “An asymmetrical cortical distribution pattern of 18F‐FDG is often reported, which can be mistaken for a cortical‐basal‐degeneration (CBD); in CBD, there is often an involvement of the basal ganglia, just unlike our case.”
